passages.happening:
‘Now when Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he was furious and filled with indignation. He ridiculed the Jews’ (verse 1) in front of his associates and the army of Samaria: “What are these feeble Jews doing? Can they restore the wall by themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they complete it in a day? Can they bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble?” (verse 2).

Tobiah, beside him, adds a joke: “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” (verse 3).

Nehemiah turns straight to God. ‘Hear us, O God, for we are despised. Turn their scorn back upon their own heads’ (verse 4). ‘Do not cover up their iniquity or let their sin be blotted out from Your sight, for they have provoked the builders’ (verse 5).

‘So we rebuilt the wall until all of it was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a mind to work’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The builders were reusing stones from heaps of rubble. Limestone that has been through fire becomes brittle and crumbles, so Sanballat's taunt about burnt stones had a point, and Tobiah's joke about the fox plays on the same fear.

In a culture of honor and shame, public ridicule in front of an army was a political weapon, meant to break a people's will before a blow was struck.

Nehemiah's prayer breaks into the story in the middle of the action. That is typical of his memoir: short prayers spoken straight to God, then back to the work. And verse 6 is the answer to the mockery. The wall rises to half its height, because the people had a mind to work.
passages.later:
A psalm prays in the same words for people who are scorned: ‘Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy, for we have endured much contempt’ (Psalm 123:3).

Jeremiah prayed against those who plotted against him in words close to Nehemiah's: ‘Do not wipe out their guilt or blot out their sin from Your sight’ (Jeremiah 18:23).
passages.hard:
How can Nehemiah pray that his enemies' sin not be blotted out?

To modern readers, and especially in the light of Jesus' command to pray for enemies, verses 4 and 5 sound harsh. A few things help to read them in context. The prayer hands vengeance to God instead of taking it. Nehemiah does not attack Sanballat; he keeps building, and he arms the people only for defense. His opponents were not just personal rivals but were trying to stop the restoration of God's city, and he treats their contempt as an offense against God. The prayer also echoes the psalms that cry out against enemies and the prayers of Jeremiah, which take a cry for justice to the only one who can judge rightly.

Christian readers differ on how far such prayers remain models. Some see them as true cries for justice that the church can still pray against persistent, unrepentant evil. Others see them as honest but pre-Christian responses that the gospel's call to love enemies now transforms. Most agree that the Bible records them without asking readers to copy their tone lightly, and that handing a wrong over to God is better than paying it back.
passages.asks: Nehemiah answered mockery with prayer and with work. Ask what you do when people laugh at what you are trying to build. And ask whether you hand your anger to God, as he did, or keep it for yourself.

passages.t: A plot, a guard, and a call to remember the Lord
passages.happening:
When Sanballat and Tobiah, with the Arabs, the Ammonites and the people of Ashdod, hear that the gaps in the wall are being closed, they are furious, and they plot ‘to come and fight against Jerusalem and create a hindrance’ (verse 8).

‘So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night’ (verse 9).

Then the trouble comes from inside. The people of Judah say, “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall” (verse 10). The enemies boast that they will strike without warning. And the Jews living near the enemies come ‘ten times over’ to warn them (verse 12).

Nehemiah stations people by families behind the lowest and weakest parts of the wall, with swords, spears and bows. Then he speaks to the nobles, the officials and everyone else: “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The allies named in verse 7 surround Judah on every side: Samaria to the north, the Ammonites to the east, the Arabs to the south, and Ashdod, the old Philistine city, to the west.

Verse 9 puts the book's way of faith in a sentence. Nehemiah prays, and he posts a guard. The chapter gives no support to the idea that trusting God means doing nothing, or that careful planning means not trusting God.

Verse 10 is a short lament. The strength of the carriers is failing, and the rubble seems endless. Discouragement inside the camp is as dangerous as the enemy outside.

Nehemiah stations men by families, so that each man guards what he loves, and he calls them to remember the Lord. In Hebrew, to remember is more than to recall a fact. It means to bring someone to mind in a way that shapes action. Against fear he sets one thing: who God is.
passages.later: Paul showed the same pairing of trust and care on the ship to Rome. Promised that everyone aboard would survive, he still told the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved” (Acts 27:31).
passages.asks: Nehemiah prayed and posted a guard. Ask whether you lean too far one way: praying without acting, or acting without praying. And ask what fear you need to answer by remembering who God is.

passages.t: Building with one hand, holding a weapon with the other
passages.happening:
‘When our enemies heard that we were aware of their scheme and that God had frustrated it, each of us returned to his own work on the wall’ (verse 15).

From then on, half of Nehemiah's men work while the other half stand guard with spears, shields, bows and armor. ‘The laborers who carried materials worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other’ (verse 17), and each builder works with his sword at his side. The trumpeter stays beside Nehemiah. “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us!” (verse 20).

They work ‘from the break of dawn until the stars came out’ (verse 21). Nehemiah tells everyone to spend the night inside Jerusalem, so that they can guard by night and work by day. ‘So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes; each carried his weapon, even to go for water’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The plot fails because, the book says, God had frustrated it. And yet the builders still carry weapons. God's rule over events works through human watchfulness rather than replacing it.

The horn was the shofar, a ram's-horn trumpet used both in worship and in war. Its blast was the signal to gather. Many of the builders came from towns outside Jerusalem, which is why Nehemiah tells them to stay inside the city at night rather than travel home through country where they could be ambushed.

The weapons were for defense. No one in the chapter attacks anyone. The people build and guard, and the closing picture, of men sleeping in their clothes with weapons in reach, leaves the reader with the cost of the work.

‘Our God will fight for us’ (verse 20) is an old confession of Israel's, spoken by Moses at the edge of the sea.
passages.later: Moses said it to Israel at the sea: ‘The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still’ (Exodus 14:14).
passages.asks: The builders kept working with a weapon in one hand. Ask what keeps you working at something good when it is costly and dangerous. And ask who is standing guard for you, and for whom you are standing guard.
